claims.claim: 95.2 ± 0.3% of ChR2-eYFP labeled boutons co-expressed both VGluT2 and VIAAT.
claims.source: Both VGluT2 and VIAAT (95.2 ± 0.3%), VGluT2 only (2.7 ± 0.2%), and VIAAT only (0%).
claims.evidence: Quantitative data from Figure 1E showing the proportion of boutons expressing different combinations of markers.

claims.claim: Both EPSCs and IPSCs at SuM-GC synapses exhibited paired-pulse depression.
claims.source: As reported previously (Hashimotodani et al., 2018; Tabuchi et al., 2022), both EPSCs and IPSCs at SuM-GC synapses exhibited paired-pulse depression (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1F and is consistent with previous studies.

claims.claim: PPR was significantly different between EPSCs and IPSCs, with EPSCs being more depressed than IPSCs.
claims.source: Importantly, we found that PPR was significantly different between EPSCs and IPSCs; EPSCs were more depressed than IPSCs (Figure 1G; EPSC: 0.46 ± 0.03, n=8; IPSC: 0.6 ± 0.03, n=8, p<0.01, unpaired t test).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of PPR values between EPSCs and IPSCs with quantitative data and significance testing.

claims.claim: Stimulating SuM axons instead of terminals yielded similar PPR results to terminal illumination.
claims.source: To avoid this possibility, we stimulated SuM axons instead of SuM terminals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B), and obtained similar results to terminal illumination (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
claims.evidence: Experimental data from supplementary figure showing that axon stimulation produces similar results to terminal stimulation.

claims.claim: The amplitudes of the second fiber volley were comparable to that of the first fiber volley in paired-pulse stimulation.
claims.source: We found that the amplitudes of the second fiber volley was comparable to that of the first fiber volley (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that ChR2-expressing SuM fibers were activated to the same extent by paired-pulse light illumination.
claims.evidence: Extracellular recordings of fiber volleys showing no change in amplitude between first and second pulses.

claims.claim: Reducing extracellular Ca2+ concentration from 2.5 to 1 mM decreased the amplitudes of both EPSCs and IPSCs.
claims.source: Reducing extracellular Ca2+ concentration from 2.5 to 1 mM decreased the amplitudes of EPSCs and IPSCs (Figure 1H; EPSC: n=14, p<0.001, paired t test; IPSC: n=15, p<0.001, paired t test).
claims.evidence: Experimental data showing the effect of reduced extracellular calcium on synaptic responses.

claims.claim: IPSCs decreased to a greater extent than EPSCs when extracellular Ca2+ was reduced from 2.5 to 1 mM.
claims.source: Remarkably, IPSCs decreased to a greater extent than EPSCs (Figure 1I; EPSC: 45.1 ± 4.1% of reduction, n=14; IPSC: 58.2 ± 2.7% of reduction, n=15, p<0.01, unpaired t test), suggesting different Ca2+ sensitivities for glutamate and GABA release.
claims.evidence: Quantitative comparison of the reduction in EPSCs vs IPSCs with statistical testing.

claims.claim: ω-conotoxin-GVIA (N-type Ca2+ channel blocker) had no effect on EPSCs or IPSCs at SuM-GC synapses.
claims.source: We found that the application of ω-conotoxin-GVIA (ω-CgTx), an N-type Ca2+ channel blocker, had no effect on EPSCs or IPSCs at SuM-GC synapses (Figure 2A; EPSC: 92.5 ± 13.8% of baseline, n=6, p=0.53, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; IPSC: 101.7 ± 11% of baseline, n=6, p=0.89, paired t test).
claims.evidence: Pharmacological experiment showing no effect of N-type Ca2+ channel blocker on synaptic transmission.

claims.claim: ω-agatoxin-IVA (P/Q-type Ca2+ channel blocker) suppressed both EPSCs and IPSCs to the same extent at SuM-GC synapses.
claims.source: In contrast, the application of ω-agatoxin-IVA (ω-Aga-IVA), a P/Q-type Ca2+ channel blocker, suppressed both EPSCs and IPSCs to the same extent at SuM-GC synapses (Figure 2B; EPSC: 23.5 ± 4.6% of baseline, n=5, p<0.001, paired t test; IPSC: 23.9 ± 1.9% of baseline, n=6, p<0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; EPSC vs IPSC: p=0.92, unpaired t test), suggesting that both glutamate and GABA release rely on P/Q-type Ca2+ channels at SuM-GC synapses.
claims.evidence: Pharmacological experiment with statistical analysis showing P/Q-type Ca2+ channels mediate both types of transmission.

claims.claim: DCG-IV inhibited EPSCs (IC50=0.11 μM) to a greater extent than it did IPSCs (IC50=0.27 μM).
claims.source: Notably, DCG-IV inhibited EPSCs (IC50=0.11 μM) to a greater extent than it did IPSCs (IC50=0.27 μM; Figure 2C; two-way ANOVA, F1,51 = 8.1, p<0.01).
claims.evidence: Dose-response data showing differential sensitivity of EPSCs and IPSCs to group II mGluR agonist.

claims.claim: 5 μM baclofen suppressed EPSCs more than IPSCs.
claims.source: Similar results were found with the application of 5 μM GABAB receptor agonist baclofen, which suppressed EPSCs more than IPSCs (Figure 2D; EPSC: 51.6 ± 2.4% inhibition, n=8; IPSC: 38.6 ± 4.3% inhibition, n=8, p<0.05, unpaired t test).
claims.evidence: Pharmacological experiment showing differential inhibition of EPSCs vs IPSCs by GABAB receptor agonist.

claims.claim: BAPTA-AM suppressed both EPSCs and IPSCs to the same extent.
claims.source: We found that the bath application of BAPTA-AM suppressed both EPSCs and IPSCs to the same extent (EPSC: 63.4 ± 12.2% of baseline, n=7, p<0.01, paired t test; IPSC: 63.4 ± 7.8% of baseline, n=8, p<0.001, paired t test; EPSC vs. IPSC: p=0.96, unpaired t test; Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: Experimental data showing equal effect of fast Ca2+ chelator on both types of transmission.

claims.claim: EGTA-AM suppressed EPSCs but did not affect IPSCs.
claims.source: In contrast, EGTA-AM suppressed EPSCs, whereas it did not affect IPSCs (EPSC: 67.4 ± 7.2% of baseline, n=6, p<0.01, paired t test; IPSC: 93.1 ± 9.2% of baseline, n=6, p=0.40, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; EPSC vs. IPSC: p<0.05, unpaired t test; Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: Experimental data showing differential effect of slow Ca2+ chelator on EPSCs vs IPSCs.

claims.claim: The spatial coupling between Ca2+ channels and synaptic vesicles is tighter for GABA release than for glutamate release.
claims.source: These results indicate tighter coupling between Ca2+ channels and synaptic vesicles for GABA release than for glutamate release.
claims.evidence: Inference drawn from the differential effects of BAPTA-AM and EGTA-AM on EPSCs and IPSCs.

claims.claim: Minimal light stimulation detected 86 EPSC-only, 67 IPSC-only, and 19 biphasic events from 1700 trials across 17 cells.
claims.source: Using this method, we analyzed 1700 trials from 17 cells and detected 86 EPSC-only, 67 IPSC-only, and 19 biphasic events (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: Quantitative data from minimal stimulation experiments showing the distribution of response types.

claims.claim: Independent EPSCs and IPSCs are the majority of synaptic responses evoked by minimal stimulation.
claims.source: These results indicate that independent EPSCs and IPSCs are the majority of synaptic responses (Figure 3D; EPSC: 5.1 ± 0.5% probability; IPSC: 3.9 ± 0.4% probability; biphasic: 1.1 ± 0.3% probability, n=17, EPSC vs biphasic, p<0.001; IPSC vs biphasic, p<0.001, one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test).
claims.evidence: Statistical analysis showing that independent responses are significantly more common than biphasic responses.

claims.claim: The amplitudes and decay of minimal light stimulation-evoked EPSCs were not changed by application of picrotoxin.
claims.source: We found that the amplitudes and decay of minimal light stimulation-evoked EPSCs were not changed by the application of the GABAA receptor blocker picrotoxin (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Pharmacological control experiment showing that EPSCs are not contaminated by GABAergic responses.

claims.claim: The amplitudes and rise time of minimal light stimulation-evoked IPSCs were not altered by application of NBQX.
claims.source: Similarly, the amplitudes and rise time of minimal light stimulation-evoked IPSCs were not altered by application of the AMPA/kainate receptor blocker NBQX (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Pharmacological control experiment showing that IPSCs are not contaminated by glutamatergic responses.

claims.claim: The amplitudes of EPSCs and IPSCs evoked by minimal stimulation were identical to those of strontium-induced asynchronous EPSCs and IPSCs.
claims.source: Furthermore, by comparing minimal stimulation-evoked PSCs with strontium-induced asynchronous PSCs (see below), we found that the amplitudes of EPSCs and IPSCs evoked by minimal stimulation were identical to those of strontium-induced asynchronous EPSCs and IPSCs, respectively (Figure 3G), suggesting that PSCs evoked by minimal stimulation were mediated by a single vesicle release.
claims.evidence: Comparison of amplitude distributions showing that minimal stimulation evokes unitary responses.

claims.claim: The majority of asynchronous synaptic events induced by Sr2+ were EPSC-only or IPSC-only, whereas biphasic PSCs represented only a minor population.
claims.source: By repeating the light stimulation of the SuM inputs 30 times (every 10 s), we found that the majority of asynchronous synaptic events were EPSC-only or IPSC-only, whereas biphasic PSCs represented only a minor population (Figure 3F; EPSC: 27.9 ± 4.7 events; IPSC: 23.4 ± 4.2 events; biphasic: 2.5 ± 0.5 events, n=11, EPSC vs biphasic, p<0.001; IPSC vs biphasic, p<0.001, one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test).
claims.evidence: Quantitative analysis of asynchronous release events showing predominance of independent responses.

claims.claim: Almost all VGluT2-positive terminals in the GC layer co-expressed VIAAT.
claims.source: As shown previously (Uchigashima et al., 2011), double immunofluorescence revealed that almost all VGluT2-positive terminals in the GC layer co-expressed VIAAT (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: Immunofluorescence data showing colocalization of glutamatergic and GABAergic markers in terminals.

claims.claim: SuM terminals formed asymmetric and symmetric synapses, characteristic of excitatory and inhibitory synapses, respectively.
claims.source: Further post-embedding immunogold EM (Figure 4C and D) showed that these terminals formed asymmetric and symmetric synapses, characteristic of excitatory and inhibitory synapses, respectively (Figure 4C and D), confirming previous observations (Boulland et al., 2009; Soussi et al., 2010; Root et al., 2018; Billwiller et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Electron microscopy data showing morphological characteristics of synapses formed by SuM terminals.

claims.claim: A single nerve terminal formed both asymmetric and symmetric synapses on a GC soma.
claims.source: Conventional EM using serial ultrathin sections also revealed that a single nerve terminal formed both asymmetric and symmetric synapses on a GC soma (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: Serial section electron microscopy showing that individual terminals form both synapse types.

claims.claim: Retrograde tracing did not reveal any retrogradely labeled neurons in the VTA after injection into the dorsal DG.
claims.source: However, our retrograde tracing with fluorescent microspheres injected into the dorsal DG did not reveal any retrogradely labeled neurons in the VTA, while labeled neurons were successfully observed in the SuM and entorhinal cortex (EC) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Anatomical tracing experiment showing that VTA does not project to the dorsal DG in the conditions tested.

claims.claim: The majority of VGluT2-positive terminals (52.5%) were associated with both GluN1 and GABAAα1.
claims.source: Specifically, the majority of VGluT2-positive terminals were associated with both GluN1 and GABAAα1 (52.5%), and the remainder were associated with GABAAα1 (22.1%) alone or GluN1 (25.4%) alone (Figure 4I).
claims.evidence: Quantitative immunofluorescence analysis showing the distribution of postsynaptic markers at SuM terminals.

claims.claim: The average distance between GluN1 and GABAAα1 clusters adjacent to the same VGluT2-positive terminal was 397.5 ± 8.75 nm.
claims.source: On average, the distance was 397.5 ± 8.75 nm, and most VGluT2-positive terminals (79.2%, 191 out of 241) form glutamatergic and GABAergic synapses within 500 nm (Figure 4J).
claims.evidence: Quantitative morphological analysis of the spatial relationship between glutamatergic and GABAergic postsynaptic sites.

claims.claim: Trains of 10 light stimuli at 5, 10, and 20 Hz elicited pronounced short-term synaptic depression of EPSCs with stronger depression at higher frequencies.
claims.source: We found that trains of 10 light stimuli at 5, 10, and 20 Hz elicited pronounced short-term synaptic depression of EPSCs during train with stronger depression at higher frequencies (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: Electrophysiological data showing frequency-dependent depression of glutamatergic transmission.

claims.claim: IPSCs exhibited short-term synaptic depression across all tested frequencies, but GABAergic co-transmission showed a similar magnitude of depression across all frequencies.
claims.source: In marked contrast to EPSCs, while IPSCs also exhibited short-term synaptic depression across all tested frequencies, GABAergic co-transmission showed a similar magnitude of depression across all frequencies (Figure 5D and E).
claims.evidence: Electrophysiological data showing frequency-independent depression of GABAergic transmission.

claims.claim: The depression of EPSCs was stronger than that of IPSCs at 10 Hz and 20 Hz.
claims.source: Indeed, comparing the amplitudes of the 10th EPSCs with those of the 10th IPSCs indicated that the depression of EPSCs was stronger than that of IPSCs at 10 Hz and 20 Hz (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: Quantitative comparison of the magnitude of depression between EPSCs and IPSCs at different frequencies.

claims.claim: 10 Hz train light illumination induced a stronger depression of EPSCs than of IPSCs when recorded simultaneously.
claims.source: We found that 10 Hz train light illumination induced a stronger depression of EPSCs than of IPSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), thereby decreasing the EPSC/IPSC ratio during the high-frequency train stimulation.
claims.evidence: Simultaneous recording of EPSCs and IPSCs showing differential depression during train stimulation.

claims.claim: The fiber volley induced by trains of 10 light stimuli was comparable across all tested frequencies.
claims.source: We confirmed that the fiber volley induced by trains of 10 light stimuli was comparable across all tested frequencies (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), indicating that a similar number of SuM fibers were activated with each light pulse during trains.
claims.evidence: Extracellular recordings showing consistent fiber activation across different stimulation frequencies.

claims.claim: Short-term depression of EPSCs with high-frequency light stimulation (10 Hz and 20 Hz) was not affected by γDGG.
claims.source: Under these conditions, short-term depression with high-frequency light stimulation (10 Hz and 20 Hz) was not affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, B).
claims.evidence: Pharmacological experiment ruling out postsynaptic AMPA receptor saturation/desensitization as the mechanism of depression.

claims.claim: Short-term depression of IPSCs in response to 10 light pulses at 10 Hz and 20 Hz did not differ before and after the application of TPMPA.
claims.source: We found that 300 μM TPMPA reduced the amplitude of IPSCs (47.1 ± 3.8% reduction, n=11, p<0.01, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), while short-term depression of IPSCs in response to 10 light pulses at 10 Hz and 20 Hz did not differ before and after the application of TPMPA (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C, D), excluding the involvement of GABAA receptor saturation in the short-term depression of IPSCs at SuM-GC synapses, suggesting a presynaptic origin of this short-term plasticity.
claims.evidence: Pharmacological experiment ruling out postsynaptic GABAA receptor saturation as the mechanism of depression.

claims.claim: Paired light illumination significantly enhanced GC firing compared to sinusoidal current injections without light stimulation at 5 Hz.
claims.source: Paired light illumination significantly enhanced GC firing compared to sinusoidal current injections without light stimulation throughout the trial (10 stimuli; Figure 6A and D).
claims.evidence: Current-clamp recordings showing that SuM activation enhances granule cell firing at 5 Hz.

claims.claim: The probability of spikes further increased when GABAergic transmission was blocked by picrotoxin at 5 Hz stimulation.
claims.source: Notably, the probability of spikes further increased when GABAergic transmission was blocked by picrotoxin (Figure 6A and D).
claims.evidence: Pharmacological experiment showing that GABAergic co-transmission limits the excitatory effect of SuM inputs at 5 Hz.

claims.claim: At higher frequencies (10 Hz and 20 Hz), the enhancement of spike probability by SuM activation was attenuated and disappeared in the last few stimulations.
claims.source: In striking contrast, at higher frequencies (10 Hz and 20 Hz), the enhancement of spike probability by SuM activation was attenuated and disappeared in the last few stimulations (Figure 6B, C, E and F).
claims.evidence: Current-clamp recordings showing frequency-dependent filtering of SuM excitatory effects.

claims.claim: In the presence of picrotoxin, SuM activation by light stimulation enhanced GC firing even in the last few stimulations at 10 Hz and 20 Hz.
claims.source: Importantly, in the presence of picrotoxin, SuM activation by light stimulation enhanced GC firing, even in the last few stimulations (Figure 6B, C, E and F), suggesting that SuM glutamatergic co-transmission still exerted excitatory effects in the later cycle, even during the short-term depression of glutamate release.
claims.evidence: Pharmacological experiment showing that GABAergic co-transmission filters out excitatory effects at high frequencies.

claims.claim: Glutamate and GABA are co-released from different synaptic vesicles within the SuM terminals.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that glutamate and GABA are co-released from different synaptic vesicles within the SuM terminals, and reveal that distinct transmission modes of glutamate/GABA co-release serve as frequency-dependent filters of SuM inputs.
claims.evidence: Summary statement in the abstract integrating multiple lines of evidence from the study.

claims.claim: Distinct transmission modes of glutamate/GABA co-release serve as frequency-dependent filters of SuM inputs.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that glutamate and GABA are co-released from different synaptic vesicles within the SuM terminals, and reveal that distinct transmission modes of glutamate/GABA co-release serve as frequency-dependent filters of SuM inputs.
claims.evidence: Summary statement in the abstract integrating the functional implications of the findings.

claims.claim: The co-release of glutamate and GABA has been identified in several brain regions of the adult brain.
claims.source: The co-release of glutamate and GABA, both fast-acting and functionally opposing neurotransmitters, has recently been identified in several brain regions of the adult brain (Trudeau and El Mestikawy, 2018; Kim and Sabatini, 2022; Wallace and Sabatini, 2023).
claims.evidence: Statement supported by citations to review articles on glutamate/GABA co-release.

claims.claim: The lateral habenula neurons receive glutamate/GABA co-releasing synaptic inputs from the entopeduncular nucleus.
claims.source: The lateral habenula neurons receive glutamate/GABA co-releasing synaptic inputs from the entopeduncular nucleus (EP) (Shabel et al., 2014; Wallace et al., 2017; Root et al., 2018) and ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Root et al., 2014; Yoo et al., 2016; Root et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Statement about anatomical connectivity supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Hypothalamic supramammillary nucleus (SuM) neurons projecting to the DG co-release glutamate and GABA.
claims.source: Hypothalamic supramammillary nucleus (SuM) neurons projecting to the DG also co-release glutamate and GABA (Pedersen et al., 2017; Hashimotodani et al., 2018; Billwiller et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Ajibola et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Statement about SuM-DG co-release supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Electrophysiological studies have demonstrated the co-packaging of glutamate and GABA in the same synaptic vesicles at EP-lateral habenular synapses.
claims.source: Previous electrophysiological studies have demonstrated that both glutamate and GABA are co-packaged in the same synaptic vesicles in the lateral habenula (Shabel et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Statement about findings in lateral habenula supported by citations.

claims.claim: An immuno-EM study demonstrated that glutamatergic and GABAergic vesicle populations are segregated in the axon terminals of the EP and VTA projections in the lateral habenula.
claims.source: Conversely, an immunoelectron microscopy (immuno-EM) study demonstrated that glutamatergic and GABAergic vesicle populations are segregated in the axon terminals of the EP and VTA projections in the lateral habenula, and that single terminals form both excitatory and inhibitory synapses (Root et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Statement about anatomical findings in lateral habenula supported by citation.

claims.claim: Glutamate and GABA are segregated into distinct vesicle populations within the axon terminals of the SuM projections in the DG.
claims.source: The same study also reported that glutamate and GABA are segregated into distinct vesicle populations within the axon terminals of the SuM projections in the DG (Root et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Statement about anatomical findings in DG supported by citation.

claims.claim: The mode of co-release of glutamate and GABA from the SuM terminals has never been functionally addressed.
claims.source: However, the mode of co-release of glutamate and GABA from the SuM terminals has never been functionally addressed.
claims.evidence: Statement identifying a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claims.claim: Different PPRs between co-transmission of dual-neurotransmitters are found in the retina (acetylcholine and GABA) and striatum (dopamine and glutamate or GABA).
claims.source: Different release properties of dual-neurotransmitter neurons have been reported in other synaptic circuits. Different PPRs (Lee et al., 2010; Silm et al., 2019; Zych and Ford, 2022) and Ca2+-sensitivities (Lee et al., 2010; Zych and Ford, 2022) between co-transmission of dual-neurotransmitters are found in the retina (acetylcholine and GABA) and striatum (dopamine and glutamate or GABA).
claims.evidence: Statement about findings in other brain regions supported by citations.

claims.claim: Different reliance on Ca2+ channels for distinct neurotransmitters have been reported in the retina, striatum, and hippocampus.
claims.source: Different reliance on Ca2+ channels for distinct neurotransmitters have been reported in the retina (acetylcholine and GABA; Lee et al., 2010), striatum (dopamine and glutamate; Silm et al., 2019), and hippocampus (acetylcholine and GABA; Takács et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Statement about findings in other brain regions supported by citations.

claims.claim: Differential release properties of two neurotransmitters indicate a separate release from distinct vesicle pools.
claims.source: These differential release properties of the two neurotransmitters indicate a separate release from distinct vesicle pools (Lee et al., 2010; Takács et al., 2018; Silm et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Interpretive statement about the implications of differential release properties, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The excitatory transmission of SuM-CA2 pyramidal neuron synapses is mediated by P/Q-type Ca2+ channels.
claims.source: Interestingly, the excitatory transmission of SuM-CA2 pyramidal neuron synapses, an exclusive glutamatergic synapse (Chen et al., 2020), is also mediated by P/Q-type Ca2+ channels (Robert et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Statement about findings at a different synapse type supported by citations.

claims.claim: Neurotransmitter release from SuM neurons depends on P/Q-type Ca2+ channels, irrespective of the target neurons.
claims.source: Therefore, neurotransmitter release from SuM neurons depends on P/Q-type Ca2+ channels, irrespective of the target neurons.
claims.evidence: Inference drawn from comparing findings at SuM-GC and SuM-CA2 synapses.

claims.claim: A previous biochemical study detected VGluT2 and VIAAT in distinct purified synaptic vesicles from the hippocampus.
claims.source: A previous biochemical study detected VGluT2 and VIAAT in distinct purified synaptic vesicles from the hippocampus (Boulland et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Statement about biochemical findings supported by citation.

claims.claim: Differences in transport mechanisms between glutamatergic and GABAergic vesicles have been reported.
claims.source: Moreover, differences in transport mechanisms between glutamatergic and GABAergic vesicles have been reported (Farsi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Statement about vesicle transport mechanisms supported by citation.

claims.claim: The theta-rhythm in the hippocampus is associated with synchronized SuM activity.
claims.source: The fact that the theta-rhythm in the hippocampus is associated with synchronized SuM activity (Kirk and McNaughton, 1991; Kocsis and Vertes, 1994; Ito et al., 2018; Farrell et al., 2021) has important implications for the low-pass filtering of this synapse.
claims.evidence: Statement about SuM activity patterns supported by citations.

claims.claim: SuM inputs may transfer their train information exclusively at the theta frequency, which could contribute to theta-mediated information processing in SuM-hippocampal circuits.
claims.source: As SuM inputs act as excitatory at 5 Hz (theta) train stimulation, but not at higher frequencies, SuM inputs may transfer their train information exclusively at the theta frequency, which could contribute to theta-mediated information processing in SuM-hippocampal circuits and their relevant brain functions, including cognitive, sleep, and navigation processes (Pedersen et al., 2017; Billwiller et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Farrell et al., 2021; Kesner et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Speculative statement about functional implications supported by citations to relevant studies.

claims.claim: Low-pass filtering of SuM inputs could prevent the over-excitation of GCs, leading to anti-seizure effects.
claims.source: In addition to SuM inputs, GCs receive EC inputs as the main excitatory inputs for discharge, and other excitatory inputs from hilar mossy cells (Hashimotodani et al., 2017). Therefore, low-pass filtering of SuM inputs could prevent the over-excitation of GCs, leading to anti-seizure effects.
claims.evidence: Speculative statement about potential functional consequences of the findings.

claims.claim: Long-term potentiation at SuM-GC synapses selectively occurs of glutamatergic co-transmission.
claims.source: In contrast to the presynaptic origin of short-term plasticity at SuM-GC synapses, we previously demonstrated the postsynaptically induced long-term potentiation at SuM-GC synapses, which selectively occurs of glutamatergic co-transmission (Hirai et al., 2022; Tabuchi et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Statement about previous findings from the same group supported by citations.

claims.claim: SuM inputs play diverse roles in modulating GC output via short- and long-term plasticity with pre- and postsynaptic distinct mechanisms.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that SuM inputs play diverse roles in modulating GC output via short- and long-term plasticity with pre- and postsynaptic distinct mechanisms, respectively.
claims.evidence: Summary statement integrating current findings with previous work.

claims.claim: C57BL/6 and VGluT2-Cre mice of either sex aged 6–7 weeks were used for electrophysiological experiments.
claims.source: C57BL/6 and VGluT2-Cre mice (Jackson Labs, Slc17a6tm2(cre)Lowl/J, stock #016963) of either sex aged 6–7 weeks were used for electrophysiological experiments and male C57BL/6 mice at 2–3 months of age were used for anatomical experiments (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Description of experimental animals used in the study.

claims.claim: 200 nL of AAV1-EF1a-DIO-hChR2(H134R)-eYFP was injected into the SuM at specific stereotaxic coordinates.
claims.source: 200 nL of AAV1-EF1a-DIO-hChR2(H134R)-eYFP (Addgene) was injected into the SuM (relative to bregma, AP: −2.2 mm, ML: ±0.5 mm, DV: −4.85 mm) at a rate of 50 nL/min.
claims.evidence: Description of viral injection procedure with specific parameters.

claims.claim: Acute transverse hippocampal slices (300-μm-thick) were prepared from mice 3–4 weeks after AAV injection.
claims.source: Acute transverse hippocampal slices (300-μm-thick) were prepared from mice 3–4 weeks after AAV injection.
claims.evidence: Description of slice preparation timing and thickness.

claims.claim: Whole-cell recordings were made from GCs using an infrared differential interference contrast microscopy.
claims.source: Whole-cell recordings using an EPC10 (HEKA Electronik) or IPA amplifier (Sutter Instruments) were made from GCs using an infrared differential interference contrast microscopy (IR-DIC, Olympus, BX51WI).
claims.evidence: Description of electrophysiological recording methods.

claims.claim: ChR2-expressing SuM fibers were activated by a pulse of 470 nm blue light (1–5ms duration, 5.0–10.5 mW/mm2).
claims.source: ChR2-expresing SuM fibers were activated at 0.05 Hz by a pulse of 470 nm blue light (1–5ms duration, 5.0–10.5 mW/mm2) delivered through a 40× objective attached to a microscope using an LED (Mightex or ThorLabs).
claims.evidence: Description of optogenetic stimulation parameters.

results.result: ChR2 was successfully expressed in SuM neurons of VGluT2-Cre mice, and the vast majority (95.2%) of ChR2-eYFP-expressing SuM boutons in the DG co-expressed both VGluT2 and VIAAT.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 provide converging evidence from viral injection methodology (C1), immunofluorescence imaging (C2), and quantitative analysis (C3) demonstrating successful targeting and co-expression of glutamatergic and GABAergic markers in SuM terminals. The quantitative data and imaging evidence are consistent with previous literature.

results.result: Glutamatergic and GABAergic transmission at SuM-GC synapses exhibit different paired-pulse ratios, with EPSCs showing stronger depression (PPR=0.46) than IPSCs (PPR=0.6), and this difference is not due to ChR2 artifacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7 demonstrate differential PPR between EPSCs and IPSCs with appropriate controls. C6 shows axon stimulation yields similar results to terminal stimulation, and C7 demonstrates that fiber volleys remain constant during paired-pulse stimulation, ruling out ChR2 desensitization. The statistical analysis (p<0.01) supports the significance of the difference.

results.result: Reducing extracellular Ca2+ from 2.5 to 1 mM decreased both EPSCs and IPSCs, but IPSCs showed greater reduction (58.2%) than EPSCs (45.1%), indicating different Ca2+ sensitivities for glutamate and GABA release.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 provide experimental evidence with statistical support (p<0.01) showing differential Ca2+ sensitivity between the two transmission types. The data are internally consistent and the inference about different Ca2+ sensitivities is reasonable given the differential reduction observed.

results.result: Both glutamate and GABA release at SuM-GC synapses depend on P/Q-type Ca2+ channels but not N-type Ca2+ channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 provide pharmacological evidence with appropriate controls. The lack of effect of ω-CgTx (C10) is validated by showing it works at CA3-CA1 synapses (Figure 2—supplement 1). The equal suppression by ω-Aga-IVA of both EPSCs and IPSCs (C11) with statistical support (p=0.92 for comparison) demonstrates shared dependence on P/Q-type channels.

results.result: Group II mGluR agonist DCG-IV and GABAB receptor agonist baclofen differentially inhibit glutamatergic transmission more strongly than GABAergic transmission at SuM-GC synapses.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13 provide dose-response data (C12) and pharmacological evidence (C13) with statistical support showing differential presynaptic modulation. The IC50 values differ significantly (0.11 μM vs 0.27 μM for DCG-IV), and baclofen shows differential inhibition (51.6% vs 38.6%, p<0.05).

results.result: Ca2+ channel-vesicle coupling is tighter for GABA release than for glutamate release, as demonstrated by differential effects of fast (BAPTA-AM) and slow (EGTA-AM) Ca2+ chelators.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 provide experimental evidence showing BAPTA-AM suppresses both transmissions equally (C14), while EGTA-AM selectively suppresses EPSCs but not IPSCs (C15, p<0.05). The inference about tighter coupling for GABA (C16) is well-supported by the classical interpretation of differential BAPTA/EGTA sensitivity.

results.result: Minimal light stimulation reveals that independent EPSCs and IPSCs are the majority of synaptic responses (86 EPSC-only, 67 IPSC-only, 19 biphasic from 1700 trials), with biphasic responses representing only a minor population.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C21 provide converging evidence from minimal stimulation experiments. The quantitative data (C17-C18) show statistical significance (p<0.001), and appropriate controls (C19-C20) rule out contamination between response types. Comparison with strontium-induced responses (C21) validates that minimal stimulation evokes unitary responses.

results.result: Asynchronous release induced by Sr2+ substitution predominantly produces independent EPSCs and IPSCs, with biphasic responses representing only a minor population.
results.evaluation: Claim C22 provides complementary evidence to the minimal stimulation experiments using a different approach (Sr2+ substitution). The statistical analysis (p<0.001) supports that biphasic responses are significantly less frequent than independent responses, strengthening the conclusion about segregated vesicle pools.

results.result: SuM terminals in the DG co-express VGluT2 and VIAAT, form both asymmetric and symmetric synapses on individual GC somata, and represent the primary source of VGluT2-positive terminals in the GC layer.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C26 provide anatomical evidence from multiple EM techniques. The immunofluorescence (C23), post-embedding EM (C24), and serial section EM (C25) converge on the conclusion that single terminals form both synapse types. The retrograde tracing (C26) rules out VTA as a significant contributor, supporting that most VGluT2/VIAAT terminals are from SuM.

results.result: The majority of VGluT2-positive SuM terminals (52.5%) are associated with both GluN1 and GABAAα1 postsynaptic markers, with an average distance of 397.5 nm between glutamatergic and GABAergic postsynaptic sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C28 provide quantitative immunofluorescence data showing spatial segregation of postsynaptic sites. The authors acknowledge potential underestimation due to the 100-nm section thickness, suggesting the actual percentage may be higher. The distance measurements provide quantitative support for spatially distinct but proximal synapses.

results.result: Glutamatergic transmission exhibits frequency-dependent depression (stronger at higher frequencies), while GABAergic transmission shows frequency-independent stable depression, resulting in a decreased EPSC/IPSC ratio during high-frequency stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 provide comprehensive evidence for differential short-term plasticity. The frequency-dependent depression of EPSCs (C29) contrasts with frequency-independent depression of IPSCs (C30), with statistical support (C31, p<0.05 at 10 and 20 Hz). Simultaneous recording (C32) confirms the differential depression, and fiber volley recordings (C33) rule out presynaptic activation differences.

results.result: Short-term depression of both EPSCs and IPSCs at SuM-GC synapses is of presynaptic origin, not due to postsynaptic receptor saturation or desensitization.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 provide pharmacological controls ruling out postsynaptic mechanisms. γDGG does not affect EPSC depression (C34), and TPMPA does not affect IPSC depression (C35), supporting a presynaptic origin. These controls are essential for interpreting the short-term plasticity results.

results.result: SuM inputs enhance granule cell firing in a frequency-dependent manner: at 5 Hz, SuM activation enhances firing throughout the train, while at 10 and 20 Hz, the enhancement is attenuated in later stimulations due to GABAergic co-transmission filtering.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39 demonstrate the functional consequences of differential short-term plasticity. At 5 Hz, SuM enhances firing (C36), with GABAergic transmission limiting this enhancement (C37). At higher frequencies (C38), the enhancement disappears in later stimulations, but blocking GABAergic transmission with picrotoxin restores enhancement (C39), demonstrating frequency-dependent filtering.

results.result: Glutamate and GABA are co-released from different synaptic vesicles within SuM terminals, and distinct transmission modes serve as frequency-dependent filters of SuM inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 represent the main conclusions integrating multiple lines of evidence: differential release properties (PPR, Ca2+ sensitivity, presynaptic modulation, Ca2+ channel coupling), independent unitary responses, anatomical segregation of postsynaptic sites, and differential short-term plasticity. The convergence of electrophysiological, pharmacological, and anatomical evidence strongly supports these conclusions.

results.result: The literature establishes that glutamate/GABA co-release occurs in multiple brain regions including lateral habenula and dentate gyrus, but the mode of co-release at SuM-DG synapses has not been functionally characterized despite anatomical evidence for vesicle segregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C48 provide appropriate literature context. The citations support the existence of glutamate/GABA co-release in multiple regions (C42-C44), conflicting evidence about vesicle packaging in lateral habenula (C45-C46), anatomical evidence for segregation in DG (C47), and identification of the knowledge gap (C48) that the current study addresses.

results.result: Differential release properties of dual-neurotransmitter neurons in other brain regions (retina, striatum, hippocampus) indicate separate release from distinct vesicle pools.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 provide relevant comparative context from other brain regions showing that differential release properties (PPR, Ca2+ sensitivity, Ca2+ channel dependence) indicate separate vesicle pools. This literature context supports the interpretation of similar findings in the current study.

results.result: Neurotransmitter release from SuM neurons depends on P/Q-type Ca2+ channels regardless of target neurons, as shown by comparison with SuM-CA2 synapses.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 provide comparative context showing that P/Q-type Ca2+ channel dependence is a general property of SuM neurons. The inference (C53) is reasonable given the evidence from both SuM-GC (current study) and SuM-CA2 synapses (cited work).

results.result: Previous biochemical and transport studies support the segregation of VGluT2 and VIAAT into distinct synaptic vesicles.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 cite relevant biochemical evidence supporting the possibility of vesicle segregation. These citations provide additional support for the interpretation of the current findings.

results.result: The frequency-dependent filtering of SuM inputs may contribute to theta-mediated information processing and prevent over-excitation of granule cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 are speculative about functional implications. While C56 provides cited evidence for theta-rhythm association with SuM activity, C57 and C58 are explicitly speculative ('may transfer', 'could contribute', 'could prevent') about the functional consequences. These hypotheses are reasonable but require additional experimental validation.

results.result: SuM inputs modulate granule cell output through both short-term plasticity (presynaptic) and long-term potentiation (postsynaptic) with distinct mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60 integrate current findings with previous work from the same group. The contrast between presynaptic short-term plasticity (current study) and postsynaptic long-term potentiation (previous work) is well-supported by citations and provides a comprehensive view of SuM-GC synaptic plasticity.

results.result: The experimental methods employed appropriate animal models, viral injection parameters, slice preparation, and electrophysiological recording techniques.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 describe standard methodological approaches with appropriate detail. The use of VGluT2-Cre mice (C61), specific viral injection parameters (C62), standard slice preparation (C63), and well-established recording techniques (C64-C65) are all appropriate for the experimental goals.

results.result: The vast majority (95.2 ± 0.3%) of ChR2-eYFP-expressing SuM boutons in the DG co-expressed both VGluT2 and VIAAT, confirming that SuM terminals contain both glutamatergic and GABAergic markers.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept this anatomical characterization without question. Reviewer 2 explicitly states the study provides 'compelling evidence at the anatomical and physiological levels,' and the editor notes the study uses 'complementary electrophysiological and anatomical experimental approaches' that are convincing.

results.result: Both EPSCs and IPSCs at SuM-GC synapses exhibited paired-pulse depression, but EPSCs showed significantly stronger depression (PPR 0.46 ± 0.03) than IPSCs (PPR 0.6 ± 0.03). This differential PPR was confirmed using both terminal and axon stimulation, with fiber volley recordings showing consistent presynaptic activation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the evidence for separate vesicle pools. Reviewer 2 notes the study demonstrates 'distinct differences in paired-pulse ratio' between glutamate and GABA transmission. The control experiments (axon stimulation, fiber volleys) are not questioned.

results.result: Reducing extracellular Ca2+ from 2.5 to 1 mM decreased both EPSCs and IPSCs, but IPSCs showed greater reduction (58.2 ± 2.7%) than EPSCs (45.1 ± 4.1%), suggesting different Ca2+ sensitivities for glutamate and GABA release.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as evidence for differential release properties. Reviewer 2 explicitly mentions the study found 'distinct differences in...Ca2+ sensitivity' between the two transmitters. This finding contributes to the overall conclusion about separate vesicle pools.

results.result: N-type Ca2+ channel blocker (ω-conotoxin-GVIA) had no effect on either EPSCs or IPSCs, while P/Q-type Ca2+ channel blocker (ω-agatoxin-IVA) suppressed both EPSCs and IPSCs to the same extent (~23-24% of baseline), indicating both transmitters rely on P/Q-type Ca2+ channels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these pharmacological findings. The shared reliance on P/Q-type channels is accepted as part of the characterization of the synapse, though it does not distinguish between vesicle pools.

results.result: Group II mGluR agonist DCG-IV inhibited EPSCs (IC50=0.11 μM) more than IPSCs (IC50=0.27 μM), and GABAB receptor agonist baclofen suppressed EPSCs (51.6 ± 2.4%) more than IPSCs (38.6 ± 4.3%), showing differential presynaptic receptor modulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as evidence for differential release properties. Reviewer 2 notes the study demonstrates 'distinct differences in...presynaptic receptor modulation' between glutamate and GABA transmission.

results.result: Fast Ca2+ chelator BAPTA-AM suppressed both EPSCs and IPSCs equally, while slow chelator EGTA-AM suppressed EPSCs but not IPSCs, indicating tighter spatial coupling between Ca2+ channels and synaptic vesicles for GABA release than for glutamate release.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as key evidence for separate vesicle pools with different spatial arrangements. Reviewer 2 explicitly mentions 'distinct...Ca2+ channel-vesicle coupling configuration for each neurotransmitter.' This is treated as strong evidence for the main conclusion.

results.result: Minimal light stimulation experiments detected predominantly independent EPSC-only (5.1 ± 0.5% probability) and IPSC-only (3.9 ± 0.4% probability) responses, with biphasic responses being rare (1.1 ± 0.3% probability). Pharmacological controls confirmed these responses were not contaminated, and amplitude analysis suggested unitary vesicle release.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these minimal stimulation findings as evidence for independent release sites. Reviewer 2 notes the study shows 'glutamate/GABA co-release produces independent glutamatergic and GABAergic synaptic responses.' The controls are not questioned.

results.result: Strontium-induced asynchronous release experiments showed that the majority of events were EPSC-only (27.9 ± 4.7) or IPSC-only (23.4 ± 4.2), with biphasic events being rare (2.5 ± 0.5), confirming independent release of glutamate and GABA.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as complementary evidence for independent release. The strontium experiments are not specifically critiqued and support the same conclusion as the minimal stimulation experiments.

results.result: Electron microscopy showed that SuM terminals formed both asymmetric (excitatory) and symmetric (inhibitory) synapses, with single terminals forming both types. Immunofluorescence revealed that 52.5% of VGluT2-positive terminals were associated with both GluN1 and GABAAα1 receptors at an average distance of 397.5 ± 8.75 nm, indicating segregated postsynaptic targets.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these anatomical findings as evidence for segregated synapses from the same terminal. Reviewer 2 notes 'most SuM boutons form distinct glutamatergic and GABAergic synapses at proximity' and that the study shows 'segregated postsynaptic targets.' The editor describes this as 'convincing evidence.'

results.result: Retrograde tracing with fluorescent microspheres injected into the dorsal DG did not reveal any retrogradely labeled neurons in the VTA, while labeled neurons were observed in the SuM and entorhinal cortex.
results.evaluation: This control experiment is not questioned by reviewers. It serves to rule out VTA as a source of the observed co-transmission in the DG.

results.result: Train stimulation at 5, 10, and 20 Hz revealed that EPSCs showed frequency-dependent depression (stronger at higher frequencies), while IPSCs showed frequency-independent stable depression. At 10 and 20 Hz, EPSC depression was significantly stronger than IPSC depression, with fiber volley recordings confirming consistent presynaptic activation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as evidence for distinct short-term plasticity. Reviewer 2 explicitly states the study demonstrates 'glutamate/GABA co-transmission exhibits distinct short-term plasticity, with glutamate showing frequency-dependent depression and GABA showing frequency-independent stable depression.'

results.result: Pharmacological experiments ruled out postsynaptic receptor saturation/desensitization as the mechanism of short-term depression. γDGG did not affect EPSC depression, and TPMPA did not affect IPSC depression, suggesting presynaptic origins.
results.evaluation: These control experiments are not questioned by reviewers and support the interpretation that the observed plasticity is presynaptic in origin.

results.result: At 5 Hz, SuM activation enhanced granule cell firing throughout the train, with further enhancement when GABAergic transmission was blocked. At higher frequencies (10 and 20 Hz), the excitatory effect was attenuated and disappeared in later stimulations, but blocking GABAergic transmission with picrotoxin restored the excitatory effect, demonstrating frequency-dependent filtering.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these functional findings as demonstrating the physiological consequences of the distinct transmission modes. The editor notes the study provides 'convincing evidence that the co-release of glutamate and GABA from different vesicles within the same terminal could modulate granule cell firing in a frequency-dependent manner.'

results.result: The authors conclude that glutamate and GABA are co-released from different synaptic vesicles within SuM terminals, and that distinct transmission modes of glutamate/GABA co-release serve as frequency-dependent filters of SuM inputs.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept this main conclusion. The editor states the work provides 'convincing evidence that the co-release of glutamate and GABA from different vesicles within the same terminal could modulate granule cell firing in a frequency-dependent manner.' Reviewer 1 notes 'I came away believing that the boutons may indeed produce and release distinct types of vesicles,' though adds 'the strength of the conclusion rests on the abundance of data (approaches) rather than the decisiveness of any one approach.' Reviewer 2 states the authors 'provide compelling evidence...that glutamate and GABA are co-release by different synaptic vesicles.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C4-C7 regarding differential PPR between EPSCs and IPSCs. Both evaluations accept these findings as evidence for separate vesicle pools, with appropriate controls for ChR2 desensitization and axon vs terminal stimulation.
Perfect agreement on claims C8-C9 regarding differential Ca2+ sensitivity. Both evaluations accept this as strong evidence for distinct release properties supporting separate vesicle pools.

Perfect agreement on claims C10-C11 regarding Ca2+ channel pharmacology. Both accept the shared P/Q-type channel dependence and lack of N-type channel involvement, though this finding does not distinguish between vesicle pools.

Perfect agreement on claims C12-C13 regarding differential presynaptic modulation by DCG-IV and baclofen. Both evaluations accept this as evidence for distinct release properties between glutamate and GABA transmission.

Perfect agreement on claims C14-C16 regarding BAPTA/EGTA differential effects. Both evaluations treat this as key evidence for separate vesicle pools with different Ca2+ channel-vesicle coupling configurations.

Perfect agreement on claims C17-C21 regarding minimal stimulation experiments. Both accept these findings as evidence for independent release sites, with appropriate controls ruling out contamination between response types.
Perfect agreement on claim C22 regarding Sr2+ substitution experiments. Both accept this as complementary evidence supporting independent release from separate vesicle pools.

Perfect agreement on claims C29-C33 regarding differential short-term plasticity. Both evaluations accept the frequency-dependent depression of glutamate vs frequency-independent depression of GABA, with appropriate controls.
Perfect agreement on claims C34-C35 regarding pharmacological controls. Both accept these experiments as ruling out postsynaptic mechanisms and supporting presynaptic origin of plasticity.
Perfect agreement on claims C36-C39 regarding functional consequences of differential plasticity. Both accept these findings as demonstrating frequency-dependent modulation of granule cell firing.

Agreement on main conclusions C40-C41, though with nuanced differences. OpenEval finds the convergence of evidence strongly supports the conclusions.
